We often discuss channels, budgets, and creatives, but less often the actual destination all that traffic is sent to. And yet this is exactly where an important line is drawn: a website can be a business asset, or it can simply be a permanent expense item disguised as a “digital presence.”

- The first test is fairly strict: if paid acquisition stops, will the website retain independent value? I mean not only traffic, but also analytics, accumulated trust signals, organic entries, a contact base, reusable materials, integrations with the CRM, and processes that continue to function. If none of this exists, then the website is not compounding value.
- The second point is the zone of control. It is surprising how often a business does not own its own domain, analytics, accounts, or key access credentials. As long as everything is calm, this goes unnoticed. But in reality, such a setup makes the company dependent on the contractor and deprives it of digital autonomy. For marketing, this means that the foundation of the channel does not belong to the business owner.
- The third point is new visibility through AI systems. If the information structure is unreadable for machines, important data is hidden in images or PDFs, and services are not described as entities, the website gradually loses visibility in new search interfaces. This is no longer a matter of trend, but of digital architecture quality.

What indicators do you consider minimally sufficient to regard a website not as an expense, but as a genuine marketing asset?
